Opinion: My 4K TV is Literally Not Worth Your Life (And Yes, I Checked The Receipt)

By Chad "Turn-the-Other-Cheek" Mildew Staff Writer, The Daily Pacifist

Look, I get it. You worked hard for that flat-screen. You spent hours at the big-box store, you wrestled it into the back of your Subaru, and you mounted it on the wall just so. It’s a beautiful television. It has four times the pixels of your old one. It is a marvel of modern engineering.

But—and please, hear me out on this—it is a rectangle of plastic and glass that displays The Bachelor.

I’ve been reading a lot online recently about people who think it’s okay to use force to stop someone from taking that rectangle. These folks seem to believe that if a window breaks and a sneaker enters the premises, they suddenly transform into John Wick. They clutch their AR-15s like security blankets and shout about “rights” and “law.”

It’s adorable, really. It’s also absolutely unhinged.

Let’s break down the math here, because clearly, some of you skipped this day in school.

The Equation of Moral Clarity

If you shoot someone over a toaster, you have effectively established an exchange rate.

  • Item Stolen: Toaster ($45 at Target).
  • Action Taken: Lethal Force.
  • Implied Value: A human soul = One (1) Bagel Browner.

Do you hear how ridiculous that sounds? You are telling the universe that warm bread in the morning is worth ending a biological miracle. You are saying that the complex, irreplaceable consciousness of a living, breathing person is equivalent to a blender.

And look, I love smoothies. Smoothies are delicious. But I’m not going to turn into Rambo because someone wants to steal my NutriBullet. If a looter kicks down my door and heads for the kitchen appliances, I’m going to step aside. I might even help him carry the microwave. Why? Because I am not a psychopath, and microwaves are replaceable. Human beings are not.

The "But It's Mine!" Argument

The primary defense I hear from the "Defend-My-Stuff-With-Violence" crowd is: "It’s the principle! It’s my property!"

Oh, wow. Groundbreaking philosophy there, Plato. You possess things. Very cool.

But let’s look at the concept of "ownership" through a slightly less ego-centric lens. Everything you own is essentially on loan from the universe until you die, at which point it becomes garbage that your kids fight over or donate to a sketchy thrift store. Your PS5? Temporary. Your collection of vintage Beanie Babies? Dust magnets.

So, when you decide to play Call of Duty in real life over a gaming console, you aren’t defending your "principle." You are sacrificing your future, your freedom, and potentially your life to protect a plastic box that will be obsolete in three years. Sony releases a new console every time Saturn enters retrograde. Are you going to commit a felony every time GPU technology improves?

Insurance: The Boring Adult Solution

Have you people heard of insurance? It’s this magical financial wizardry where you pay a company a small fee, and they buy you new stuff if the old stuff gets taken.

If someone steals my car:

  1. I call the police (later, once the adrenaline wears off).
  2. I call State Farm.
  3. I get a rental and eventually a check.
  4. I do not go to prison for aggravated assault.

The "tough guys" who want to patrol their porches with baseball bats skip steps 1 through 3 and jump straight to "I am the law." It’s performative masculinity at its finest. You aren’t protecting your family; you’re protecting your fragile ego from the horror of feeling like a victim. And honestly? Being a victim of theft is way better than being a murderer. Trust me on this. The court fees for murder are astronomical; the deductible on renter's insurance is like $500.

What Would Jesus (or Gandhi) Do?

I know, I know, bringing up religion makes eyes roll. But let’s be real: almost every major spiritual tradition agrees that stuff is stupid compared to people.

Buddha literally sat under a tree and owned nothing but a bowl. Do you think if someone stole his bowl he would have roundhouse kicked them into nirvana? No. He would have meditated on the impermanence of material possessions.

Yet, we have modern "warriors" acting like the Ten Commandments were actually titled "Ten Reasons to Stand Your Ground."

Conclusion: Let Them Have the Sneakers

To summarize for the slow learners in the back:

If you kill someone to save your TV, you don’t have a hero complex. You have a priority disorder. You value objects over organisms. You are willing to destroy a family, traumatize a community, and ruin your own life just so you can keep watching Netflix on a screen you already own.

So please, put down the gun. Lock the door if it makes you feel better (it won't stop a determined looter, but it’s good cardio). Go upstairs, put on some noise-canceling headphones, and listen to a podcast about peace.

If you wake up tomorrow and your living room is empty? Relax. You’re safe. Your conscience is clean. And frankly, that ugly vase your mother-in-law gave you was dragging down the feng shui anyway.

Chad Mildew is a Senior Columnist for The Daily Pacifist. He lives in a yurt and believes that the only thing worth fighting for is the last slice of pizza, and even then, he’ll probably just split it.

Third, defending property violently during unrest ignores the broader context from which looting often emerges. In effect, property-protective violence plants seeds for greater insecurity, not stability.

In conclusion, resorting to violence during looting or unrest solely to protect private property is both morally indefensible and practically harmful. Property can be replaced through insurance, rebuilding, and community effort; life cannot. The defense of possessions does not outweigh the defense of life and human dignity, and to blur this boundary risks creating a society more violent, fractured, and insecure. This calculus is not applied in any other context of civil law; we do not allow shopkeepers to execute suspected shoplifters. The unique, volatile context of unrest does not nullify this fundamental asymmetry. The trauma and injustice of property loss are real, but they do not, and cannot, constitute a proportional ground for taking a life. The scale of the response—the irreversible violence of a bullet or a blade—overwhelms the scale of the harm it purports to prevent.

Looting and rioting are rarely acts of abstract criminality; they are symptoms of deeper pathologies: profound inequality, perceived injustice, political breakdown, and a collapse of trust in institutions. To respond to this symptom with individualized violence is to treat a fever with a hammer. It addresses none of the underlying disease. An individual property owner, acting as a self-appointed judge, jury, and executioner, becomes an agent of further social disintegration. The violence they unleash does not restore order; it fuels more violence, entrenches societal divides, and transforms a crisis of governance into a war of all against all. The property defended in blood becomes a monument to a society that chose its objects over its people.

The legal and ethical frameworks that ground property rights themselves do not support this extreme conclusion. Even in jurisdictions with robust self-defense laws, the principle of proportionality is paramount. The threat must be imminent and severe, and the response must be reasonably necessary to neutralize that threat to life or serious bodily harm. Property, while protected, generally does not meet this threshold. The "castle doctrine" in many places extends the right to defend one's home from intruders, but it is not a blanket license for violence against anyone near one's business during a riot. The law recognizes that while your home is your sanctuary, your storefront is part of a shared civic space, and the rules of engagement within it are fundamentally different. To blur this line is to advocate for a form of privatized martial law, where armed citizens enforce their own order—a recipe for chaotic, retaliatory bloodshed.

Finally, the "property defense" argument is a slippery slope into vigilantism and collective punishment. In the fog of panic and chaos, who is deemed a "looter"? Who is a legitimate target? The history of such moments shows an alarming tendency for violence to spill over racial, ethnic, and class lines, punishing entire communities for the actions of a few. The "defender" is often acting on fear and perception, not clear-eyed evidence. This creates a scenario where the violence deployed to protect property itself becomes a profound source of terror, destabilizing the community far more than the property damage ever could. It sacrifices the long-term project of a peaceful, cohesive society on the short-term altar of protecting goods.

In conclusion, to justify killing for the protection of property during unrest is to make a devastating trade: it exchanges the value of life for the value of things, ignores the root causes of the crisis, contradicts the very proportionality embedded in our legal systems, and risks unleashing a spiral of vengeance that destroys the social fabric property is meant to exist within. The defense of property is a legitimate concern, but it is not, and can never be, a sufficient justification for violence. True security is not found behind the barrel of a gun pointed at a desperate neighbor, but in the arduous, collective work of building a society where the destruction of property is rendered less likely by the preservation of dignity, justice, and shared humanity. In the heat of the moment, we must be guided not by the instinct to protect our possessions, but by the higher wisdom to protect our common humanity—a principle that, once breached, leaves us with nothing of lasting value to defend.
